#6618. Grand Theft Auto VI Welcomes a New Wave of (Virtual) Gym Bros

After a 13-year drought, Grand Theft Auto VI has finally hit the masses. Predictably, a large swath of guys have called off work to give themselves just enough time to explore the immersive fictional land of Leonida, where players can do just about everything they can in real life—from driving cars and renovating homes to playing video games within a video game. In Grand Theft Auto VI, that now also includes hitting the gym. And if you want to progress through the story as efficiently as possible, becoming an in-game gym rat might be the best thing you can do.

Expanding on a gameplay mechanic introduced in Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, working out in GTA levels up your character to help with progressing through the story. The fitter you become in the game, the more stamina you have to sprint, the more health you have before you’re Wasted, and the more focus you have to take down enemies. Just like in real life, pumping iron makes daily life a whole lot easier.

To get fit, you can use the weights in Jason’s outdoor gym, which features the big three full-body lifts: squats, bench presses, and deadlifts. While your character handles the heavy lifting, all you have to do is carefully time your button presses to complete reps without causing an injury. Once you have enough money, you can purchase memberships at gyms across the city, giving you access to treadmills, free weights, and workout machines. The exercise options are so extensive (you can even do zone 2 cardio) that gamers have already started trading tips to the best GTA 6 workouts for maximizing your character’s gains.

As your character gets stronger, their avatar transforms accordingly, developing more defined muscles, a six-pack, and even a chiseled face. Neglecting your fitness and overeating (a real thing you can do in the game) has an alternate effect as your player visibly gains weight and adopts a “dad bod.”

Inevitably there will be many players that skip the gym this weekend so they can pump a little virtual iron with their thumbs. There’s something undeniably ironic about looksmaxxing your GTA character while spending hours sitting on the couch playing a video game. But don’t think that just because it’s all on a screen that you won’t walk away from a session with a little back pain, so maybe schedule a few breaks in between. You could even build a home gym of your own like Jason’s—it’s already got one fitness expert’s approval.

#6617. Can a Pre-Nup Be Romantic?

Budgeting, filling out tax forms together, managing family dynamics, and standing in line at city hall: not sexy. Not romantic. Alas, they are the mundane mechanics of even the most thrilling of married lives. Soon after a ring is on the finger, many couples are now discussing prenups—and it’s a topic that brings up unglamorous realities.

No, the administrative process of a prenup isn’t inherently romantic, and let’s not pretend it is. But what it does for the relationship—laying everything bare with radical honesty—is deeply romantic.

“I think navigating something that’s challenging in a relationship and coming out of it aligned is romantic, sexy, and empowering,” says Ashley Hesseltine. The co-host of Girls Gotta Eat spoke openly about choosing to have a prenuptial agreement with her now husband. “But I will not lie. The process of a prenup is inherently annoying, unsexy, and invasive. And it’s admin.”

Wedding planning has a way of sweeping us up into a whirlwind of floral arrangements, seating charts, and linen swatches. Conversations about money, family expectations, and core values naturally come to the forefront next to celebrations.

Luxury wedding planner JoAnn Gregoli agrees that pausing and zooming out to address a prenuptial agreement and the structural foundation of your partnership before you even start picking a venue makes the whole planning process all the more clear. “Marriage isn’t only about romance; it’s also about finances, property, obligations, and decision-making,” she says. “When a couple confronts the subject together, they feel more like they’re entering the marriage as a team and not as a dictatorship.”

You’ve likely already experienced that deep feeling of intimacy with your partner after an exceptionally vulnerable conversation with them. This is just like that. Afterwards, wedding planning transforms from a period of financial tension into one of deep alignment.

It helps, but there’s no requirement to execute a 30-page legal document to reap the emotional rewards of the prenup talk. Some value lies in the vulnerability required to have the conversation at all.

Therapist and author Israa Nasir notes that money remains one of the ultimate taboos in modern relationships, often carrying hidden emotional baggage. “Constructive and supportive conversations can reveal parts of yourself that you otherwise might not—deeper insecurities, past experiences with financial trauma, childhood scarcity, and your relationship with money,” she says. “If your partner doesn’t understand why you behave a certain way about money, it’s harder for them to have empathy for you.”

It may feel like you’re setting up transactional boundaries or betting against your longevity. But in essence, it’s an exercise in radical honesty. Approaching your partner with curiosity rather than judgment is a quick way to turn a wobbly topic fraught with anxiety into a brick in your foundation.

Nobody’s excited about asking their partner about student loans or retirement accounts. It may feel daunting. That’s completely normal.

Start small, and don’t put the pressure on this having to be one big conversation. The first chat can just be about getting their thoughts on prenups in general. Then, you can talk about your thoughts on how you want to manage finances in your relationship. Finally, when you’re ready, you can start diving into assets and what each person wants to walk away with.

The time-old advice of there being no such thing as too much communication stands here. You can even talk about how you want to enter this conversation in a way that might make both of you feel the most comfortable. Agree to enter the discussion with empathy, zero judgment, and positive intent.

Remind yourself that you can frame this discussion around shared goals and mutual care.

Here are a couple of conversation starters:

I’m fairly certain nobody gets married to get divorced. If it does happen, state laws dictate what happens to you both. Letting state statutes dictate your shared destiny? Not romantic. An act of mutual protection? Maybe even chivalrous.

Family and divorce mediator Aswini Puvitharan highlights how modern prenups are moving away from traditional adversarial mindsets. “Prenups are often introduced as ‘How do I protect what’s mine?’ but the better starting point is ‘What would fairness and financial security look like for both of us?’ The more thoughtful prenups today reflect deep care—providing housing, financial support, or protecting someone who takes a career break to raise children.”

Protection from potential bitterness or future legal chaos is inherently loving. “It should feel like you and your partner against the prenup, not you and your partner against each other,” says Hesseltine. “It’s an insurance policy you’re probably never going to use, and if you were strong enough to figure this out together in a healthy way, chances are you’ll never need it.”

#6616. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6613. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6612. Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011. (Scott J. Ferrell/CQ Roll Call)

Former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous New York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

“Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”

West Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and New Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey said.

Rockefeller was born in New York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

He returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

In West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he said of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness."

He had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

Rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

Rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

Rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

But defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

Despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension plans.

In 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him said the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

He believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the issues. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

He viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

But industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

“The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he said on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

He had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller announced he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

Rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance plan, he said, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”

"These are people," Rockefeller said, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice."

The amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

Rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

Rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.

#6611. 14 Best Barn Coats for Men in 2026, According to GQ Editors

The best barn coats for men are a close cousin of the chore jacket—similar in spirit, but built tougher. They’re heartier, heavier, better insulated, and usually more water-resistant. Where the chore jacket belonged to the factory floor, the barn coat was made for the fields: a layer you could shrug on to tackle chores outdoors.

But ever since the ’80s and ’90s, the barn coat has been finding a new audience of urbanites who understand its utility, even on mean city streets. Today, alongside the waxy Barbour zip-ups and dad-approved L.L. Bean riffs, a ton of capital-F fashion labels—The Row, Auralee, Prada—have been herding the barn coat back into the center of the style conversation.

Reading to buy your first barn coat? Make sure it’s cut with enough room to comfortably slip a sweater beneath it, and that its craftsmanship ensures it’ll remain a reliable rotation beater for years to come. The former, of course, might demand some trial and error on your end, but the latter is exactly where we come in. These are the absolute best barn coats for men on the market right now, from the genre-defining joints you already know to the sleeper-hit versions you probably don’t.

Deep, easily accessed pockets? A warm corduroy collar? A charming plaid lining? This jacket from J.Crew is, quite simply, the platonic ideal of a barn coat. It has all the details dialed in, built upon a sturdy, 100% cotton washed canvas body that will only soften and feel more like your own in time. Originally launched over 40 years ago, there’s a reason J.Crew is still able to sell it four decades later. And we didn’t even mention the hook on the back, so you can hang this up with ease as soon as you enter your bustling, warm, overcrowded local bar. It’s the little things.

I should disclose up front that I’m a bit of an OrSlow obsessive. I own more from the brand than I’ll ever admit publicly or privately and doubt that I’ve ever been unaware of something it’s produced, but this is because no brand has more consistently lived-up to pre-purchase expectations in my illustrious shopping career, and the only things that see the light of day are things that are absolutely dialed. And this jacket is dialed, folks. Made in Japan from start to finish, it has the kind of cut that can handle a Joey Tribbiani-esque volume of layers, is made from a cotton canvas fabric that will look unreal in half a decade, and the type of construction that other brands show factories when they’re trying to describe what they’re looking for.

We couldn’t round out a piece on barn coats without a nod to L.L. Bean, one of the OGs of the style. A century ago, Bean launched a rugged duck-hunting coat that slowly shifted into a catch-all field jacket—the ancestor of the one they’re still selling today. It’s made from hefty, water-resistant canvas, with a sewn-in lining, five roomy pockets, underarm gussets, and bi-swing shoulders so you can actually move in it. And like many things Bean, the sizing is inclusive, there’s even a “Tall” option for the vertically gifted among us.

The Real McCoy’s is known for painstakingly recreating vintage garments—the Abercrombie set that Hunter S. Thompson made famous is an all-timer—so you can bank on the fact that this barn jacket has all the proper credentials. If you are dubious, however, know that it’s made out of a damn-near-bulletproof cotton canvas fabric, is fully lined with twill to trap some heat when things get chilly, has a perfect hit of corduroy at the collar and comes equipped with one of the sickest pocket configurations you’ll ever see in the genre. It’s hard to call anything “perfect,” but I feel comfortable saying that this is an ideal barn jacket, and would be hard to beat against any rubric.

What’s all this, then—a Barbour as a barn coat? The Beaufort isn’t cut from the same stiff American canvas, but the brief is identical: a country jacket for tramping through fields, feeding the chickens, or—let’s be honest—making it to the pub. King Charles even reinstated the brand’s Royal Warrant last year (he is the Menswear King, after all). Built long before DWR and Gore-Tex, its waxed cotton shrugs off rain, the oversize corduroy collar blocks the wind, and you can zip in liners or snap on a hood if you feel like accessorizing. Best detail? The little hand-warmer pockets perched above the main ones—perfect for thawing fingers after a day of grouse shooting or a lap of the Lower East Side. Just remember: it will need the occasional re-waxing, but that’s all part of the fun.

If you're getting hung up on the idea of a barn jacket that’s implicitly unqualified to do barn jacket work, this isn’t going to be the one for you. But you if think that the barn jacket can be both a highly-functional, historically-revered workwear staple AND that it’s a brilliant canvas on which the most tasteful among us can mess around a little, this one from the maniacs (complimentary) at Auralee is hypnotic. The outer is made from a cotton moleskin—which is like flannel’s heavyweight cousin, for those unfamiliar—that’s been unevenly garment-dyed to look like it’s endured thousands of miles on a tractor. Meanwhile, the pockets are flawless, the zipped placket comes outfitted with a buttoned storm flap, and the whole thing is garnished with a detachable shearling collar, just in case you thought they spared a single expense along the way.

Knickerbocker is known for tasteful pieces that can help you rebuild an entire wardrobe, and that includes this faithful homage to vintage fly-fishing wading jackets commonly worn in the jacket’s namesake upstate region. The Portuguese canvas and rounded collar stand out among other jackets on our list, and the gusseted shoulders allow for a wide range of movement on and off the river.

First off, don't fear the red colorway. It's just as easy to wear as any other fall-adjacent color and it stands out roughly twice as much, which is kind of the dream ratio for eye-catching jackets. Also, it's just a damn-good barn coat, with deep ol' hand pockets, a wind-stopping corduroy collar and endless layering potential.

This is absolutely a barn jacket. All the hallmarks are there, from the corduroy collar (more on that later) to the generous pocket situation and layout. But it's also one of the most stunning corduroy jackets on the market due to one of the most breathtaking corduroys you will ever see. And if you ever were wondering, why don't they make the whole jacket out of the collar, they do.

Filson's classic Barn-adjacent coat is an undeniable giant in the space—big ol' stow pockets, corduroy collar, canvas outer—but the insulated iteration is every bit as easy to wear and twice as warm, without adding much bulk at all.

Think of this TS joint as the ultimate "what if." Like, what if, instead of a classic canvas outer there was a super soft, ultra sturdy, almost flannel-like flocked denim? And instead of corduroy, TS threw in a leather collar? Because across the board, they decided to find out.

Much like the Auralee number up top, this isn't the kind of barn jacket that you'd be wearing to bale hay, but there's only a select few among us doing that anyways. You can, however, wear the living hell out of this all winter long, because not only does it layer beautifully, it has the requisite storage, showstopping potential and only gets better with age. Is it practical? That's not the point.

Levi’s takes a no-nonsense swing at the barn jacket—exactly what you’d expect from them. You get a sturdy shell, a quilted lining that brings just the right amount of warmth, and two generous front pockets. Sure, it skips the classic hand-warmer pockets, but at a price this good, you can afford to overlook a detail or two.

This is one of the most affordable options on this list, but you're not leaving a ton on the table if this is your prefered route. The outer is a waxed organic cotton that will hold up well against all forms of precipitation, there's a full flannel lining and the collar even buttons into a stand, to really keep things insulated.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6610. The 8 Best James Bond Films

Terrible puns. Rampant misogyny. Disposable female characters. A frequently stale rotation of vodka martinis, gun fights, and stiff-upper-lip bureaucracy. Bond movies are very easy to make fun of—and, let’s face it, of the 25 that have so far been released over the past six decades, a majority are pretty forgettable. But there are a handful that are worth watching, even if you actively abhor the subgenre.

Following Robert Pattinson’s appointment as the new 007, we present eight Bond films that are actually decent. May more follow!

Where it all began. A suave Sean Connery, Ursula Andress as the bikini-clad Honey Ryder, the pristine white beaches of Jamaica… this Terence Young-helmed first installment of the franchise laid the blueprint for everything that followed, but is also a thoroughly entertaining romp in its own right. It’s easy to see why it became a box-office bonanza and birthed a cultural phenomenon that endures to this day.

“Do you expect me to talk?” growls Connery. “No, Mr. Bond, I expect you to die!” retorts Gert Fröbe’s hulking, laser-wielding Auric Goldfinger (a role that was nearly played by Orson Welles, if you can believe it). For its quippy repartee, Shirley Bassey’s soaring opening track, a lethal bowler hat-wearing sidekick named Oddjob, and an all-female troop of pilots led by Honor Blackman, Guy Hamilton’s glittering thriller is pretty unbeatable.

George Lazenby took on the mantle—just the once; what could be chicer?—for the sixth Bond movie, a spy caper with a decidedly more romantic bent, given it features the womanizing 007 finally meeting his match in Diana Rigg’s turbulent countess. The ski chases, as crafted by director Peter R. Hunt, are thrilling, but it’s the film’s jaw-dropping, heartbreaking ending that makes it one for the ages.

On the whole, the less said about Roger Moore’s stint as Bond, the better—though I’ll make an exception for this campy riot from Lewis Gilbert. The ethereal Barbara Bach as a Soviet KGB agent? Richard Kiel’s menacing henchman Jaws, who chows down on his enemies with his giant steel teeth? (He was initially supposed to die in this film, but was so beloved by audiences at test screenings that the script was changed, allowing him to survive and return for 1979’s Moonraker.) Say no more.

Then came the dashing Timothy Dalton, whose notably more serious take on the character in this John Glen-spearheaded action epic (plus 1989’s Licence to Kill) is both impressive and criminally under-seen. The stunts are bananas, the synthy ’80s music a delight, and Maryam d’Abo a standout as a cellist who moonlights as a sniper.

Pierce Brosnan’s four outings as Bond provided diminishing returns, but the first, directed by Martin Campbell, is a memorable one thanks to a range of factors: Dame Judi Dench as the franchise’s steely new M, Sean Bean as the dastardly 006, Robbie Coltrane as a Russian gangster, Alan Cumming as a slimy computer programmer, and Famke Janssen as the hilariously evil Xenia Onatopp, as well as the clean-cut polish our new Irish leading man brings to the role.

I’ll just say it: this film, once again helmed by Martin Campbell, which introduced Daniel Craig in the part of the tormented MI6 agent, is the best of the franchise to date. It has the perfect balance of grit and gloss, Eva Green as his slippery foil, a bloody-eyed Mads Mikkelsen, and a climactic Venetian set piece that has to be seen to be believed. Incredible.

“This is the end…” Adele’s swooning vocals on her Oscar-winning title track always send a shiver down my spine, and perfectly set the tone for Sam Mendes’s gripping take on the well-worn formula. It opens with a train ride from hell and builds to a crescendo in the Scottish Highlands, with everyone from a snarling Javier Bardem to franchise newcomers Naomie Harris, Ben Whishaw, and Ralph Fiennes all getting in on the action. It’s proof that a Bond movie can tick all the requisite boxes and also be spectacular cinema. The next installment, directed by Denis Villeneuve, certainly has a lot to live up to.

#6609. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.
